Modern.brandNameRationale: Hermann Snellen, the Dutch ophthalmologist, designed the Snellen eye chart in 1862 — the universal vision-testing standard, used in every optometrist's office worldwide. The eponym is public-domain (Snellen died in 1908) and signals an optometry-led posture.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern eyewear has been crowded with DTC frame brands competing on style. The opening is for a brand that puts vision testing in the brand position — frame design built around the eye exam, not the runway.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Warby Parker (warbyparker.com) holds the considered-DTC slot. MOSCOT (moscot.com) is the heritage-American peer. Cubitts (cubitts.com) plays the heritage-British position. We sit closer to Cubitts with a sharper optometry-led identity.
Modern.positioningStatement: Modern eyewear built around the eye exam.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 50. Wears glasses daily. Visits the optometrist annually. Reads the prescription before the frame.
behaviors: Reads the prescription on the eye chart
Buys one new frame every two years

dos: Photograph the frame on a real face

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark — Snellen Frames in a precise modern grotesk with the famous Snellen 'E' tucked above the word as a hallmark. The 'E' alone is the favicon.

typography.primary: GT America for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for prescriptions and measurements
typography.rationale: One family. The mono carries the prescription, the PD, and the dimensions.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: 'Lunetier' is the French term for spectacle-maker (in use since the 17th century). Pillet evokes the Parisian Belle-Époque optical houses on the Rue de la Paix — the surname is suggestive of the era without colliding with an active mark. The pair grounds the brand in the French luxury-optical tradition.
Luxury.industrySummary: Luxury eyewear is dominated by fashion-house licensed frames. The opening is for a small atelier reviving the Parisian lunetier tradition — horn, gold, hand-bevelled lenses, made by appointment.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Jacques Marie Mage (jacquesmariemage.com) holds the haute-eyewear peer slot. Lunetterie Générale (lunetteriegenerale.com) is the considered-luxury peer. E.B. Meyrowitz (meyrowitz.uk) plays the heritage-bespoke position. We sit between Lunetterie Générale and Meyrowitz in posture.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A Parisian lunetier reviving the Belle-Époque spectacle tradition.

targetAudience.primary: 45 to 70. Owns multiple pairs of high-end frames. Visits the atelier for fitting. Will pay for horn and gold.
behaviors: Owns at least one horn frame

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark — Lunetier Pillet set in a thin neoclassical Didot with a small hand-drawn lorgnette mark above. The mark appears on the certificate and the case.

typography.primary: Didot for the wordmark and certificates
typography.secondary: Adobe Garamond for body and correspondence
typography.rationale: Didot carries the Parisian Belle-Époque tradition. Garamond keeps the correspondence warm.

Minimal.tagline: The smallest part of the spectacle.
Minimal.brandNameRationale: The rivet hinge — the small metal pin joining temple to frame-front — was invented in the mid-19th century. It is the smallest mechanical element in eyewear, and the part that fails first. Naming the brand after the smallest part signals attention to the underlying construction.
Minimal.industrySummary: Minimal eyewear has been crowded with rebranded acetate frames. The opening underneath is a brand that names the smallest engineering element — the hinge — and lets that detail define the catalog.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Mykita (mykita.com) holds the minimal-engineered slot. Götti (gotti.ch) is the Swiss-minimal peer. Lindberg (lindberg.com) sets the rimless-minimal bar. We sit closer to Götti with a sharper hinge-led identity.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Minimal eyewear named for the smallest part of the spectacle.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 55. Owns one or two pairs. Replaces only when broken. Reads the screws.
behaviors: Buys one frame every five years

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark — Rivet Hinge in a humanist sans with a single dot (the rivet) above the word. The dot alone is the favicon.

typography.primary: ABC Diatype for the wordmark and body
typography.secondary: ABC Diatype Mono for measurements and tolerances
typography.rationale: One family. Mono for the engineering data.

Corporate.tagline: Frame production and lens edging, vertically integrated.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Frame manufacturing and lens grinding are the two historical sub-trades of the optical industry — separate businesses since the 17th century. The pair names the vertical integration: both halves of the supply chain under one company.
Corporate.industrySummary: Corporate eyewear supply is split between low-cost frame importers and a few vertically integrated firms. The opening is for a B2B supplier that does both halves — frame and lens — under one contract.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: EssilorLuxottica (essilorluxottica.com) is the global giant. Marchon (marchon.com) holds the wholesale-frame peer. Safilo (safilo.com) plays the licensed-frame peer position. We sit smaller and more vertically focused than these.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Vertically integrated corporate eyewear supply — frame and lens under one contract.

targetAudience.primary: 40 to 60. Procurement directors at vision-benefits programs, independent optometrist chains, and corporate wellness platforms.

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small geometric mark — FRAME & LENS set in a tight grotesk with two small circles (a frame outline) to the left. Reads cleanly on procurement decks and trade-show banners.

typography.primary: Inter for marketing and B2B materials
typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed catalogs and contracts
typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across digital. The serif handles printed wholesale catalogs.

Creative.tagline: Every pair signed inside the temple.
Creative.brandNameRationale: In the 19th century, spectacle-makers signed their work inside the temple with an engraved cartouche — a small decorative panel bearing the maker's name and date. The word 'Cartoucheur' (the engraver of cartouches) names the practice and centers the brand on the signature inside every pair.
Creative.industrySummary: Creative eyewear has been crowded with patterned-acetate brands. The opening is for a house that signs every pair on the inside — a small engraving the wearer sees and the world doesn't.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Jacques Marie Mage (jacquesmariemage.com) holds the creative-haute peer slot. Garrett Leight (garrettleight.com) sits in the considered-creative position. Ahlem (ahlemeyewear.com) plays the Parisian-creative peer. We sit closer to Ahlem with a sharper signature-engraving identity.
Creative.positioningStatement: Creative eyewear with engraved interior cartouches — every pair signed, dated, numbered.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 55. Design-literate buyer. Owns multiple pairs of independent eyewear. Cares about provenance and signature.
behaviors: Photographs the inside of the temple

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark — Cartoucheur set in a decorative engraver's italic with a small cartouche mark (an oval ornamental panel) as the hallmark.

typography.primary: GT Sectra for the wordmark and editorial
typography.secondary: An engraver's italic for the signature line
typography.rationale: Sectra carries the catalogue register. The italic carries the signature.
